summary:
What It Is
Ofoiq (أفق, Arabic for "Horizon") is an interactive, web-based 3D Digital Twin and smart agricultural assistant designed for smallholder farmers in semi-arid regions, modeled on the agricultural landscape of Al-Nassariya farms in Nablus, Palestine. Bridging the gap between complex Earth observation datasets and practical field decisions, Ofoiq provides a dual-interface experience: a simplified, actionable dashboard for everyday growers ("Farmer Mode") and an analytical simulation workbench for agronomists and researchers ("Expert Mode").
Why It Matters
Smallholder farmers in water-scarce Mediterranean climates face intensifying heatwaves, erratic rainfall, prolonged summer droughts, pest outbreaks, and soil degradation caused by repetitive monoculture farming. Traditional farming relies on guesswork, leading to water waste, late disease detection, mistimed harvests, and declining yields. Ofoiq democratizes space data, empowering farmers to conserve water, protect crop health, and adapt to climate extremes without requiring technical expertise or expensive field hardware.
How It Addresses the Challenge
Powered by daily NASA POWER (v2.10.3) agro-climatological records—encompassing air temperatures, precipitation, wind speed, relative humidity, and surface soil moisture (GWETTOP)—integrated with the physically based Hargreaves-Samani reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) model and live 7-day weather forecasts, Ofoiq translates raw satellite metrics into clear, localized

Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

Scientific basis for a crop-rotation decision-support system — Field Shift project

Team: OFOQ | أفق · University: An-Najah National University

1. Abstract

This study analyzes 120 days of daily data for a point in Al-Nassariya (Nablus Governorate) from NASA POWER. The data show a hot, dry summer: the mean daily maximum temperature was about 40 °C in July and August, 31 days had a maximum temperature of 40 °C or higher, and daily rainfall stayed below 1 mm until 9 October. Effective rainfall began on 10 October, and total rainfall reached only 32.9 mm by 11 November. Surface soil wetness (GWETTOP) rose from 0.09 to a peak of 0.41 after the rain. A quality check revealed a non-physical discontinuity in root-zone wetness (GWETROOT) on 1 October; we therefore do not rely on the current "soil moisture status" classification until it has been verified. The only source actually used in the analysis is NASA POWER; SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GLDAS and GAEZ are planned integrations and are not yet used.

2. Study Area and Data

  • Location: Al-Nassariya, Nablus, a single point (latitude 32.2438, longitude 35.39).
  • Source: NASA POWER, daily/point API, version v2.10.3, AG community. Downloaded on 15 November 2026.
  • Period: 15 July – 15 November 2026 was requested. The last day returned by the server is 11 November, so the total is 120 days, with no missing values (the fill value is -999).
  • Variables downloaded: T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN and T2M (°C); RH2M (%); WS10M (m/s); GWETTOP and GWETROOT (surface and root-zone soil wetness, 0 to 1); PRECTOTCORR (mm/day).
  • Derived variables: daily temperature range (T2M_MAX − T2M_MIN), cumulative rainfall, soil-status classification, and quality flags.
  • Sources not yet used: The data file lists SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GLDAS and GAEZ as "reference only"; all soil moisture and rainfall values in the file come from POWER.

3. Methodology

  • The daily series was aggregated by month (July covers 15–31 only, and November covers 1–11 only).
  • Event indicators: number of days with maximum temperature ≥ 35 °C and ≥ 40 °C, date of the first rainfall ≥ 1 mm, and length of the dry spell.
  • Soil-status classification follows the team's thresholds on GWETROOT: Dry below 0.35, Wet at 0.60 or above, and Moderate in between.
  • Quality flags defined by the team: "Flat run" if the value stays constant for 14 days, and "Jump" if it changes by more than 0.10 in one day.
  • All numbers can be reproduced from the JSON and XLSX files, and the Metadata contains the full request link.

4.2 Temperature

The maximum temperature peaked at 43.04 °C in August. A total of 31 days recorded a maximum of 40 °C or higher, and 71 days recorded 35 °C or higher. The first day on which the maximum fell below 30 °C was 2 October. The daily temperature range dropped from about 17 °C in July and August to about 10.5 °C in October and November. The lowest minimum temperature was 7.9 °C on 10 November, so there is no indication of frost in this period, although winter has not yet entered the series.

4.3 Relative Humidity and Wind

Monthly mean RH2M rose from 43.9% in July to about 55% in October and November, with a daily maximum of 75.8% on 7 November. Wind speed fell from about 2.9 m/s in July and August to about 1.8 m/s in October and November.

4.4 Rainfall

  • The total was 32.92 mm over 120 days: practically zero in July and September, and 0.01 mm in August.
  • The first rainfall ≥ 1 mm came on 10 October (3.19 mm), followed by 2.03 mm and 4.02 mm on 11 and 12 October. The preceding dry spell was therefore at least 87 consecutive days (the series starts on 15 July).
  • A second wave occurred on 26–27 October (1.68 and 3.83 mm) and a third on 6–8 November.
  • All of November's rain (13.77 mm) fell on 6–8 November, and the largest daily value was 6.95 mm on 7 November.
  • There were 26 days with rainfall greater than zero, but only 8 days with ≥ 1 mm.

4.5 Soil Moisture

Surface wetness (GWETTOP) stayed between 0.09 and 0.12 from July to September, then ranged between 0.18 and 0.41 in October and November, peaking at 0.41 on 7 November with the heaviest rainfall. This behavior is plausible: the surface layer dries out in summer and responds directly to rain.

4.6 Data Quality: A Discontinuity in GWETROOT

  • GWETROOT stayed constant at 0.45 from 15 July to 30 September (78 days), despite the high temperatures and absence of rain. The entire series contains only 5 distinct values (0.30, 0.31, 0.32, 0.34 and 0.45).
  • On 1 October it dropped from 0.45 to 0.31 in a single day, while GWETTOP rose from 0.09 to 0.20 and that day's rainfall was only 0.08 mm. This is a sudden change that rainfall cannot explain.
  • Effect on the classification: every day from 15 July to 30 September (78 days) was classified "Moderate," and every day from 1 October to 11 November (42 days) was classified "Dry," with no "Wet" days. In other words, the classification says the soil became drier after the rains began, which is misleading.
  • We could not determine the cause from the file. Hypotheses that need verification include a change in the data source or its processing at the month boundary, or that root-zone values in these products do not respond to daily events as expected. This should be checked against the NASA POWER documentation and by comparison with GLDAS and SMAP.
  • Credit goes to the team: the "Flat run" and "Jump" flags caught the problem automatically.

5. Discussion and Relevance to Crop Rotation

The current data are not sufficient to favor one crop rotation over another, but they identify indicators that can feed the comparison of the three strategies (the current rotation plus two proposed rotations):

  • End of the dry summer: A dry spell of ≥ 87 days and a maximum temperature ≥ 40 °C on most days of July and August imply water and heat stress on any summer crop, and reliance on irrigation. The actual state of vegetation cover cannot be determined from these data (it requires NDVI from Landsat, Sentinel-2 or MODIS).
  • Start of the rainy season: The first effective rain came on 10 October, with intermittent rainfall afterwards. Rain-onset date and cumulative rainfall are valid indicators for a planting window; the final decision belongs to a local agricultural engineer.
  • Autumn temperatures: The maximum fell to about 25 °C and the minimum to about 15 °C in early November. The suitability of particular crops for these conditions should be assessed with reference sources (such as GAEZ), not from these data alone.
  • Diseases: RH2M is a daily mean and does not reflect nighttime humidity or leaf wetness. In this period only 5 days combined T2M between 15 and 22 °C with RH2M ≥ 60%. This is not enough to draw any conclusion about disease risk, so we suggest postponing the early-warning feature until winter data and hourly data are available.
  • Proposed indicators for the comparison engine: rain-onset date, cumulative rainfall, number of days with temperature ≥ 35/40 °C, dry-spell lengths, and a water-deficit index (rainfall minus reference evapotranspiration, ET0). ET0 can be roughly estimated with the Hargreaves-Samani method from maximum and minimum temperature and latitude alone .

6. Limitations and Risks

  • Single point and coarse grid: POWER data are gridded, and the spatial resolution of the meteorological inputs is, to the best of our knowledge, tens of kilometers , so differences between fields on the plain and the effects of elevation and terrain are not captured.
  • No ground measurements: Temperature and rainfall were not compared against a weather station or a local rain gauge.
  • Short, unrepresentative period: Four months of a single year, covering summer and the start of the rains but not the main winter season, so the region's climate cannot be characterized and no comparison with the historical average is possible.
  • Soil thresholds: The 0.35 and 0.60 thresholds were chosen by the team and have no scientific reference yet, and the GWET value is an approximate ratio, not volumetric moisture.
  • GWETROOT discontinuity: This currently prevents reliance on the soil classification (Section 4.6).
  • RH2M is a daily mean and does not represent nighttime conditions or leaf wetness.
  • POWER latency: The last available day is 11 November.
  • Sources not integrated: SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GLDAS and GAEZ were not used in this analysis.
  • The results are indicators of weather and soil conditions; they do not prove the existence of stress or disease in the fields, and they are a support tool that does not replace the expertise of the farmer and the agricultural engineer.

7. Recommendations and Next Steps

Before submission:

  • Do not present "Soil Moisture Status" as a final result, or present it labeled "under verification."
  • Replace the old chart in the research file (2022 data) with Figure 1 from this data.
  • State clearly that POWER is the only source actually used and that the rest are future integrations.
  • Include the limitations section (Section 6) in the paper.

Afterwards:

  • Download a longer POWER series to build a reference climate and compute anomalies instead of absolute thresholds, and to cover the winter season through spring.
  • Compare GWETROOT with GLDAS and SMAP, and explain the discontinuity.
  • Compare temperature and rainfall with a nearby Palestinian weather station.
  • Compute ET0 and the water-deficit index, and link them to the rotation comparison.
  • Add NDVI (Landsat or Sentinel-2) to show variability within the plain.
